about: Graph Studio (docs/apmicro-spec.md section 6, builder T1). Content for microeconomics/assets/tools/graph-studio.js; the model is microeconomics/assets/tools/math/graph-studio.js and the validator scripts/lib/apmicro-tool-checks/graph-studio.mjs. graphs[] are the eleven graphs (id -> ApMicroGraph kind in the model's KIND), each with what shifts its curves and the spec Explore opens on (free). scenarios[] are what happens: shifts (curve and direction, checked against the validator's own SHIFTER table), a line (key side, to or at), a point (key at a named point or a PPC region), an area to shade (an ApMicroGraph region), and check[] choice steps (four options, the first right, one reason each). contexts[] are the drills, one per graph or policy family, each served when its topic is published. Words in {braces} come from names[graph].
intro: The graph point is the one students lose most often on the AP® Microeconomics exam. Graph Studio has every graph the course draws: the PPC, supply and demand, surplus and policy (price controls, taxes, subsidies and trade), the cost curves, the competitive firm beside its market, monopoly, monopolistic competition, the labor market beside its firm, monopsony, externalities and the Lorenz curve. Pick a graph, pick what happens, and draw it yourself: shift a curve, mark a point, move a price line, or tap the areas to shade. Test yourself grades every graph point by point, the way readers score it, and names the slip when a point is lost.
howItWorks:
Explore. Choose a graph, then choose what happens. Drag the curve you think moves (or use its button and the arrow keys), tap where the point belongs, drag the price line, or tap each part of an area to shade it. The picture says at once whether you have it, and a wrong try names what you drew instead (the market quantity in place of the efficient one, the price read from MR, the rectangle that stops at the old quantity). Show me draws the answer, and Why walks through it. With nothing picked, a graph is yours to play with: tap any area to see what it is called.

Test yourself. Each problem is one graph, built one rubric point at a time: the labels (when you draw it from scratch), the shift, the new equilibrium, the price or wage line, the point, the shaded area, and sometimes a question about what the graph means. The strip on the graph ticks each point you earn on the first try. The PPC and supply-and-demand drills are free; the other graphs' drills are part of Premium, and Explore draws every graph for everyone.

Graphs are drawn on a 0 to 10 grid with straight demand and supply curves, and the cost curves come from one cubic total cost, so marginal cost always crosses AVC and ATC at their lowest points. Shift size is never graded, only the curve and its direction.

settings.costs: A firm that makes {good}, in the short run.
settings.pc: A perfectly competitive market for {good}, and one firm in it.
settings.monopoly: The only seller of {good} in a town.
settings.monocomp: A {shop} in a town with many {shop}s, each a little different.
settings.labor: A competitive market for {job}s, and one {firm} that hires them.
settings.monopsony: The only employer of {job}s in a remote town.

graphs.title: Production possibilities curve
graphs.shows: Every combination of two goods an economy can make with all its resources and today's technology.
graphs.axes: Each axis is one of the two goods, by name. The curve bows out because resources are not equally good at making both goods, so the opportunity cost of each good rises as more of it is made.

list: Out: more or better resources (labor, capital, land), more human capital, better technology
In: resources lost (a disaster, a war), technology lost

graphs.movement: Moving resources from one good to the other is a movement along the curve, and the opportunity cost is the other good given up. A point inside means unemployed or wasted resources; a point outside cannot be reached now.

graphs.title: Supply and demand
graphs.shows: Buyers' demand and sellers' supply in one market; they cross at the equilibrium price and quantity.
graphs.axes: Price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. Mark the equilibrium price and quantity on the axes (P1, Q1, then P2, Q2 after a change).

list: Tastes and preferences
Income (normal and inferior goods)
Prices of substitutes and complements
Number of buyers
Expected future prices
Input prices
Technology
Number of sellers
Taxes and subsidies on sellers
Expected future prices
Prices of other goods the sellers could make

graphs.movement: A change in the good's own price is a movement along demand and supply, not a shift: compare the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied at that price. Anything else that changes what buyers want or what sellers offer shifts a whole curve.

graphs.title: Surplus and policy
graphs.shows: One market with the areas that measure who gains: consumer surplus, producer surplus, and what a price control, a tax, a subsidy, trade or a tariff does to them.
graphs.axes: Price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. A policy line (a ceiling, a floor, the world price) is horizontal and labeled on the price axis; a per-unit tax or subsidy shifts supply by the amount per unit.

list: A per-unit tax on sellers: left (up) by the tax
A per-unit subsidy to sellers: right (down) by the subsidy
The same shifters as any demand curve

graphs.movement: Consumer surplus is under demand and above the price buyers pay; producer surplus is above supply and below the price sellers keep, each out to the quantity actually traded. Deadweight loss is the surplus no one gets, between demand and supply from the quantity traded to the efficient quantity.

graphs.title: Cost curves
graphs.shows: A firm's short-run marginal cost and average costs, from one total cost.
graphs.axes: Cost (or price and cost) on the vertical axis, the firm's quantity of output on the horizontal axis.

list: Up: a per-unit tax or a higher input price per unit (MC, AVC and ATC all rise)
Down: cheaper inputs per unit, better technology
Up: a lump-sum tax, a license fee, higher rent (a fixed cost: ATC and AFC rise, MC and AVC stay put)
Down: a lower fixed cost

graphs.movement: MC crosses AVC and ATC at their lowest points: while the next unit costs less than the average it pulls the average down, and once it costs more it pulls the average up. The bottom of AVC is the shutdown point; the bottom of ATC is the break-even point.

graphs.title: Perfect competition: market and firm
graphs.shows: The market sets the price where demand meets supply; the firm takes that price as its horizontal demand, d = MR = AR = P, and produces where P = MC.
graphs.axes: Market: price and quantity (Q). Firm: price and cost, and the firm's quantity (q, lower case). The price is carried across from the market to the firm.

list: Market demand: the usual demand shifters
Market supply: input prices, technology, and firms entering (right) or leaving (left)

graphs.movement: Above minimum ATC the firm earns an economic profit and new firms enter, shifting market supply right until the price falls to minimum ATC. Below it firms lose money and some leave. Below minimum AVC a firm shuts down even in the short run.

graphs.title: Monopoly
graphs.shows: One seller facing the whole downward-sloping market demand, with marginal revenue below it.
graphs.axes: Price and cost on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. MR starts where demand does and falls twice as fast.

list: Demand for the product (MR moves with it)
Per-unit costs (ATC moves with it)
Fixed costs alone

graphs.movement: The monopolist makes the quantity where MR = MC, then charges the price read up on the demand curve. It makes less and charges more than the allocatively efficient point, where demand meets MC, and the triangle between them is the deadweight loss.

graphs.title: Monopolistic competition
graphs.shows: One firm among many selling different versions of a product: a downward-sloping demand that entry and exit move.
graphs.axes: Price and cost on the vertical axis, the firm's quantity on the horizontal axis.

list: Left: rivals enter while there is economic profit
Right: rivals leave while there are losses

graphs.movement: In the short run the firm acts like a small monopoly: MR = MC, price from demand, a profit or loss box. In the long run entry and exit move its demand until it just touches ATC: zero economic profit, a price above MC, and excess capacity (output below the bottom of ATC).

graphs.title: Competitive labor market and firm
graphs.shows: The market wage set by labor demand and supply, and one firm that takes that wage and hires where MRP equals it.
graphs.axes: Wage on the vertical axis, quantity of labor on the horizontal axis, in both panels. The wage is carried across to the firm as its labor supply, S = MFC = W.

list: The price of the product (MRP = MP x P)
Workers' productivity (MP)
The prices of other inputs
Number of workers
Wages in other jobs
Preferences about work and leisure
The same as labor demand: the firm's MRP is its demand for labor

graphs.movement: Labor demand is derived demand: a change in product demand changes the product price, so MRP, so the demand for labor. The firm hires where MRP = MRC, and for a price taker in the labor market MRC is the wage.

graphs.title: Monopsony
graphs.shows: The only employer in a labor market: to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for all, so its marginal factor cost lies above labor supply.
graphs.axes: Wage on the vertical axis, quantity of labor on the horizontal axis.

list: Product price and productivity
Number of workers in the town (MFC moves with it)

graphs.movement: The monopsonist hires where MRP = MFC, then pays the wage read down on the labor supply curve at that number. It hires fewer workers and pays less than a competitive market would.

graphs.title: Externality
graphs.shows: A market whose buyers or sellers ignore a cost or benefit to other people: the private curves set the market quantity, the social curves the efficient one.
graphs.axes: Price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. Label the private curves (D = MPB, S = MPC) and the social curve (MSC or MSB).

list: Left by the external cost: a per-unit (Pigouvian) tax on a negative production externality
Right by the external benefit: a per-unit subsidy to buyers of a good with a positive consumption externality

graphs.movement: A negative externality makes the market produce too much; a positive one, too little. The deadweight loss is the triangle between the social and private curves from the market quantity to the efficient one. A corrective tax or subsidy equal to the external cost or benefit moves the market to the efficient quantity.

graphs.title: Lorenz curve
graphs.shows: The share of income earned by each share of households, from the poorest up.
graphs.axes: Cumulative percentage of households on the horizontal axis, cumulative percentage of income on the vertical axis.

list: Toward equality: progressive taxes, transfers, wider access to education
Away from equality: wages that diverge, a regressive tax

graphs.movement: The farther the Lorenz curve bows below the line of equality, the more unequal incomes are. The Gini coefficient is the area between them divided by the whole triangle under the line of equality.

scenarios.title: Better technology
scenarios.cause: A new technology raises productivity in making both {x} and {y}.
why: With better technology the same resources make more of both goods, so every point on the curve moves out.
That is economic growth: combinations that were out of reach become possible.

scenarios.title: More workers
scenarios.cause: Many new workers join the labor force.
why: More of a resource lets the economy make more of both goods, so the curve shifts out.

scenarios.title: A flood
scenarios.cause: A flood destroys factories and farmland.
why: With fewer resources the economy can make less of both goods, so the whole curve shifts in.

scenarios.title: A recession
scenarios.cause: A recession leaves many workers without jobs and factories idle.

point.label: X
point.ask: where the economy is during the recession.
point.why: inside the curve: with resources unemployed, the economy makes less than it could.

scenarios.title: Every resource in use
scenarios.cause: Every worker and machine is used, and nothing is wasted.

point.label: X
point.ask: a combination the economy makes with full, efficient use of its resources.
point.why: on the curve: full employment of resources is productive efficiency, and more of one good now costs some of the other.

scenarios.title: Out of reach
scenarios.cause: Planners ask for more of both goods than the economy can make today.

point.label: X
point.ask: a combination the economy cannot make with today's resources and technology.
point.why: outside the curve: it cannot be reached until the curve shifts out.

scenarios.title: Incomes rise
scenarios.cause: Incomes rise, and buyers treat {good} as a normal good.
scenarios.because: higher income for a normal good

slips.S: Income changes what buyers want, not what sellers offer: a rise in income for a normal good shifts demand right.

why: Buyers with more income want more of a normal good at every price, so demand shifts right.
At the old price there is now a shortage, so the price rises until the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied are equal again.

scenarios.title: A substitute costs more
scenarios.cause: The price of {sub}, a substitute for {good}, rises.
scenarios.because: a higher price of a substitute
why: When a substitute costs more, some buyers switch to {good}, so demand for {good} shifts right.

scenarios.title: A complement costs more
scenarios.cause: The price of {comp}, which people use with {good}, rises.
scenarios.because: a higher price of a complement
why: Goods used together are bought together: when the price of {comp} rises, buyers want a smaller quantity of {good} at every price, so demand shifts left.

scenarios.title: Out of fashion
scenarios.cause: A popular report makes {good} less fashionable.
why: A change in tastes changes how much buyers want at every price: demand shifts left.

scenarios.title: More buyers
scenarios.cause: Thousands of new residents move to the town.
why: More buyers means more is wanted at every price, so demand shifts right.

scenarios.title: A price rise expected
scenarios.cause: Buyers expect {good} to cost more next month.
why: Buyers who expect a higher price later buy more now, so today's demand shifts right.

scenarios.title: An input costs more
scenarios.cause: The price of {input}, an input for {good}, rises sharply.

slips.D: An input price changes what it costs sellers to make the good, not what buyers want: it shifts supply.

why: Each unit costs more to make, so sellers offer less at every price: supply shifts left.
At the old price there is now a shortage, so the price rises and the quantity falls.

scenarios.title: Better technology
scenarios.cause: A new machine lets sellers make {good} faster and more cheaply.
why: Lower costs per unit let sellers offer more at every price, so supply shifts right.

scenarios.title: More sellers
scenarios.cause: Several new sellers open in the market.
why: More sellers offer more at every price: supply shifts right.

scenarios.title: Its own price falls
scenarios.cause: The price of {good} falls, and buyers buy a larger quantity.
why: The price is on the vertical axis, so a change in it moves the market along demand: the quantity demanded changes, demand does not.

scenarios.title: Its own price rises
scenarios.cause: The price of {good} rises, and sellers offer a larger quantity for sale.
why: A higher price moves sellers along their supply curve: the quantity supplied rises, supply does not shift.

scenarios.title: Consumer surplus
scenarios.cause: The market is at its equilibrium.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Consumer surplus is the triangle under demand and above the equilibrium price, from zero to the equilibrium quantity: what buyers were willing to pay beyond what they paid.

scenarios.title: Producer surplus
scenarios.cause: The market is at its equilibrium.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below the equilibrium price, from zero to the equilibrium quantity: what sellers received beyond the least they would accept.

scenarios.title: Total surplus
scenarios.cause: The market is at its equilibrium.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus: the whole area between demand and supply out to the equilibrium quantity. It is largest at the competitive equilibrium.

scenarios.title: A binding price ceiling
scenarios.cause: The city caps the price of {good} below the equilibrium price.

line.why: A ceiling only binds below the equilibrium price; above it, it changes nothing.

scenarios.ask: The graph now shows the ceiling. Shade the deadweight loss.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Under the ceiling only the quantity sellers supply is traded. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and supply from that quantity out to the equilibrium quantity.

scenarios.title: Consumer surplus under a ceiling
scenarios.cause: A price ceiling holds the price of {good} below the equilibrium price.
scenarios.ask: Shade consumer surplus with the ceiling in place.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Buyers who get the good pay the ceiling price, so consumer surplus is under demand and above the ceiling, out to the smaller quantity sellers supply: it gains the rectangle that was producer surplus and loses its part of the deadweight loss.

check.label: What happens in this market at the ceiling price?
options: A shortage: the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied
A surplus: the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded
Nothing: the market stays at its equilibrium quantity
Supply shifts left until the market clears
why: Yes. Below the equilibrium price buyers want more than sellers offer: compare the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied at the ceiling.
A surplus comes from a price held above equilibrium, a floor. A ceiling below it leaves buyers wanting more than sellers offer.
A binding ceiling stops the price from rising to equilibrium, so the market cannot get back there.
A price ceiling moves the market along supply to a smaller quantity; nothing shifts supply.

scenarios.title: A binding price floor
scenarios.cause: The government sets a minimum price for {good} above the equilibrium price.

line.why: A floor only binds above the equilibrium price; below it, it changes nothing.

scenarios.ask: The graph now shows the floor. Shade the deadweight loss.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Under the floor only the quantity buyers demand is traded. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and supply from that quantity out to the equilibrium quantity.

scenarios.title: Producer surplus under a floor
scenarios.cause: A price floor holds the price of {good} above the equilibrium price.
scenarios.ask: Shade producer surplus with the floor in place, assuming sellers make only what buyers buy.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Sellers who sell get the floor price, so producer surplus is above supply and below the floor, out to the smaller quantity buyers demand.

scenarios.title: A per-unit tax
scenarios.cause: The government puts a per-unit tax on sellers of {good}.
scenarios.askShift: Draw the tax: shift the curve it moves, the way it moves it.

slips.D: The tax is paid by sellers, so it raises their cost of each unit: supply shifts up (left) by the tax, and demand stays put.

scenarios.shadeWhy: Tax revenue is the tax per unit times the quantity after the tax: the rectangle between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, out to the new quantity.
why: The tax makes buyers pay more and sellers keep less, and both sides trade less: that lost trade is the deadweight loss.

scenarios.title: Deadweight loss of a tax
scenarios.cause: A per-unit tax on sellers of {good} is in place.
scenarios.ask: Shade the deadweight loss of the tax.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The tax cuts the quantity traded below the equilibrium quantity. The lost surplus is the triangle between demand and supply from the quantity after the tax to the old equilibrium.

scenarios.title: Who pays a tax
scenarios.cause: A per-unit tax on sellers of {good} is in place.
scenarios.ask: Shade the part of the tax revenue paid by buyers.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Buyers pay the rise in their price, from the old equilibrium price up to the price they pay now, on every unit still sold.

scenarios.title: A per-unit subsidy
scenarios.cause: The government pays sellers a subsidy for each unit of {good} they sell.
scenarios.askShift: Draw the subsidy: shift the curve it moves, the way it moves it.
scenarios.ask: Shade the cost of the subsidy to the government.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The government pays the subsidy on every unit sold after it: the rectangle between the price sellers receive and the price buyers pay, out to the new, larger quantity.

scenarios.title: Deadweight loss of a subsidy
scenarios.cause: A per-unit subsidy to sellers of {good} is in place.
scenarios.ask: Shade the deadweight loss of the subsidy.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The subsidy pushes the quantity past the efficient one. Each extra unit costs more to make than buyers value it: the triangle between supply and demand beyond the old equilibrium quantity.

scenarios.title: Gains from free trade
scenarios.cause: The country opens to trade, and the world price of {good} is below its domestic price.
scenarios.ask: Shade the gain in total surplus from trade.
scenarios.shadeWhy: At the lower world price buyers gain more than domestic sellers lose. The net gain is the triangle between demand and supply over the imports.

check.label: At the world price, how much does the country import?
options: The quantity demanded minus the quantity supplied at home
The quantity supplied at home
The old equilibrium quantity
The quantity demanded at home
why: Yes. Buyers want more than home sellers offer at the world price, and imports fill the gap.
That is what home sellers make; imports are the rest of what buyers want.
The old equilibrium no longer holds at the world price.
That is what buyers want in all; home sellers supply part of it.

scenarios.title: Producer surplus with trade
scenarios.cause: The country imports {good} at a world price below its domestic price.
scenarios.ask: Shade domestic producer surplus at the world price.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Home sellers get the world price, so producer surplus is above supply and below the world price, out to the quantity they supply.

scenarios.title: Tariff revenue
scenarios.cause: The country puts a per-unit tariff on imported {good}.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The tariff is collected on imports only: the rectangle between the world price and the price with the tariff, over the imports after the tariff.

scenarios.title: Deadweight loss of a tariff
scenarios.cause: The country puts a per-unit tariff on imported {good}.
scenarios.ask: Shade the deadweight loss of the tariff.
scenarios.shadeWhy: A tariff costs two triangles: home sellers making units the world makes more cheaply, and buyers giving up units they valued above the world price.

scenarios.title: A per-unit tax
scenarios.cause: The government taxes each unit of {good} the firm makes.

slips.ATC: A per-unit tax raises the cost of every unit, including the next one, so MC shifts up (and AVC and ATC with it). ATC alone moves for a fixed cost.

why: A cost paid on each unit adds to the cost of the next unit: MC, AVC and ATC all shift up.

scenarios.title: A license fee
scenarios.cause: The city charges the firm a yearly license fee, the same however much it makes.

slips.MC: A lump-sum fee does not change what one more unit costs, so MC and AVC stay put. Only the fixed part rises: ATC and AFC shift up.

why: A fixed cost is spread over the units made: AFC and ATC rise, but the cost of one more unit, MC, does not.

scenarios.title: Cheaper materials
scenarios.cause: The materials used in each unit of {good} get cheaper.

slips.ATC: Cheaper materials lower the cost of every unit, including the next one, so MC shifts down (with AVC and ATC).

why: A lower cost on each unit lowers MC, AVC and ATC together.

scenarios.title: Lower rent
scenarios.cause: The landlord lowers the firm's monthly rent.

slips.MC: Rent is the same however much the firm makes, so the cost of one more unit does not change: MC stays put and ATC shifts down.

why: Lower rent lowers the fixed cost spread over each unit: AFC and ATC fall, MC and AVC do not.

scenarios.title: Where MC meets ATC
scenarios.cause: Look at how MC and ATC meet.

point.label: X
point.ask: where MC crosses ATC.
point.why: where MC crosses ATC: the bottom of ATC. While MC is below the average it pulls the average down; once above, it pulls it up.

scenarios.title: The shutdown point
scenarios.cause: The price of {good} keeps falling.

point.label: X
point.ask: the shutdown point: the lowest price at which the firm still produces in the short run.
point.why: the bottom of AVC, where MC crosses it. Below that price the firm cannot even cover its variable costs, so it loses less by shutting down.

scenarios.title: Minimum efficient scale
scenarios.setting: A firm choosing its size in the long run.
scenarios.cause: In the long run the firm can choose any plant size.

point.label: X
point.ask: the lowest point of long-run average total cost.
point.why: the bottom of LRATC. To its left are economies of scale (costs per unit fall as the firm grows); to its right, diseconomies of scale.

scenarios.title: Market demand rises
scenarios.cause: Market demand for {good} rises.

slips.MC: The firm's costs did not change: market demand shifts in the market panel, and the higher price reaches the firm as a higher price line.

line.why: The firm is a price taker: its demand is the horizontal line at the new market price, d = MR = AR = P.

point.label: X
point.ask: the quantity the firm makes now.
point.why: where the new price line crosses MC: P = MC.

scenarios.shadeWhy: Profit is the rectangle between the price and ATC at the quantity where P = MC, from zero to that quantity.
why: With the price above minimum ATC the firm earns an economic profit. In the long run that draws new firms in, shifting market supply right until the price is back at minimum ATC.

scenarios.title: Market demand falls
scenarios.cause: Market demand for {good} falls.

line.why: The firm takes the new, lower market price as its horizontal demand, d = MR = AR = P.

point.label: X
point.ask: the quantity the firm makes now.
point.why: where the lower price line crosses MC.

scenarios.shadeWhy: The loss is the rectangle between ATC and the price at the quantity where P = MC, from zero to that quantity.
why: The price is still above minimum AVC, so the firm keeps producing in the short run. In the long run some firms leave, shifting market supply left until the price is back at minimum ATC.

scenarios.title: A bumper harvest
scenarios.cause: Good weather brings a bumper harvest of {good} across the market.

line.why: The lower market price becomes the firm's horizontal demand, d = MR = AR = P.

point.label: X
point.ask: the quantity the firm makes now.
point.why: where the lower price line crosses MC.

scenarios.shadeWhy: The price is below ATC at the firm's quantity: the loss is the rectangle between ATC and the price, from zero to that quantity.

scenarios.title: Firms enter
scenarios.cause: Firms are earning economic profits, so in the long run new firms enter the market.

slips.D: Entry adds sellers, so it shifts market supply, not demand. Firms enter because of economic profit, not because demand rises.

line.why: The firm takes the lower long-run price as its horizontal demand.

point.label: X
point.ask: the quantity the firm makes in the long run.
point.why: where P = MC, which is now the bottom of ATC: zero economic profit, and no more reason to enter.

scenarios.title: A profitable price
scenarios.cause: The market price is above the firm's minimum ATC.

point.label: X
point.ask: the quantity the firm makes.
point.why: where the price line, d = MR = AR = P, crosses MC.

scenarios.shadeWhy: Profit is (P minus ATC) times q at the quantity where P = MC: the rectangle between the price and ATC, from zero to that q. Not at the bottom of ATC.

scenarios.title: A price below ATC
scenarios.cause: The market price is below the firm's minimum ATC but above its minimum AVC.

point.label: X
point.ask: the quantity the firm makes in the short run.
point.why: where the price line crosses MC: the loss is smallest there.

scenarios.shadeWhy: The loss is the rectangle between ATC and the price at the quantity where P = MC.

check.label: Should the firm keep producing in the short run?
options: Yes: the price is above AVC, so it covers its variable costs and part of its fixed costs
No: any firm with an economic loss shuts down at once
No: the price is below minimum ATC, which is the shutdown point
Yes, but only if the price is above ATC
why: Yes. Shut down and it still pays its fixed costs; produce and the price covers AVC with some left over toward them, so it loses less.
In the short run the fixed costs are paid either way. A firm keeps producing while the price covers AVC.
The shutdown point is the bottom of AVC, not of ATC. Below ATC but above AVC the firm produces at a loss.
Above ATC the firm would earn a profit. Here it has a loss and still produces, because the price covers AVC.

scenarios.title: The shutdown price
scenarios.cause: Think about how low the market price could fall before this firm stops producing.

point.label: X
point.ask: the firm's shutdown point.
point.why: the bottom of AVC, where MC crosses it. Below that price, revenue does not even cover variable costs.

scenarios.title: The monopoly's choice
scenarios.cause: The monopolist picks the quantity and price that maximize its profit.

point.label: M
point.ask: the monopolist's quantity and price.
point.why: at the quantity where MR = MC, priced straight up on the demand curve (not on MR or MC).

scenarios.shadeWhy: Profit is the rectangle between the price (on demand) and ATC at the quantity where MR = MC, from zero to that quantity.

scenarios.title: Deadweight loss of monopoly
scenarios.cause: The monopolist charges its profit-maximizing price.
scenarios.ask: Shade the deadweight loss of monopoly.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The monopolist stops at the quantity where MR = MC, short of the efficient quantity where demand meets MC. The lost surplus is the triangle between demand and MC over those units.

scenarios.title: Consumer surplus under monopoly
scenarios.cause: The monopolist charges its profit-maximizing price.
scenarios.shadeWhy: Consumer surplus is under demand and above the monopoly price, out to the monopoly quantity.

scenarios.title: Demand rises
scenarios.cause: Demand for {good} rises.

slips.MC: Demand changed, not the firm's costs: demand shifts right, and MR moves with it.

point.label: M
point.ask: the monopolist's new quantity and price.
point.why: at the new quantity where MR = MC (MR moved right with demand), priced up on the new demand curve.

scenarios.title: The socially optimal point
scenarios.cause: A regulator wants the monopolist to produce the allocatively efficient quantity.

point.label: E
point.ask: the allocatively efficient (socially optimal) quantity and price.
point.why: where demand meets MC: P = MC, so the last unit is worth exactly what it costs to make.

scenarios.title: The most revenue
scenarios.cause: The monopolist's manager wants the most total revenue, not the most profit.

point.label: R
point.ask: the quantity and price that give the most total revenue.
point.why: where MR = 0: one more unit adds nothing to revenue. That is the unit-elastic point of demand.

scenarios.title: A fair-return price
scenarios.setting: A natural monopoly: the town's only water company.
scenarios.cause: Average total cost keeps falling over the whole demand, so one firm serves the market most cheaply. A regulator sets a fair-return price.

point.label: F
point.ask: the fair-return price and quantity.
point.why: where demand meets ATC: P = ATC, so the firm covers its costs and earns zero economic profit.

check.label: Why not make the natural monopoly charge P = MC?
options: With ATC above MC, a price equal to MC is below ATC, so the firm would lose money
Because P = MC is where profit is largest
Because at P = MC there would be a shortage
Because MC is above demand at every quantity
why: Yes. ATC keeps falling, so MC is below ATC: at P = MC the firm could not cover its costs without a subsidy.
Profit is largest where MR = MC, not where P = MC.
The regulated price is on demand, so buyers get what they want at it: no shortage.
Demand is above MC over most of the graph; that is why P = MC gives a large quantity.

scenarios.title: Short-run profit
scenarios.cause: The {shop} has a new idea its rivals have not copied yet.

point.label: M
point.ask: the firm's quantity and price.
point.why: where MR = MC, priced up on demand.

scenarios.shadeWhy: The rectangle between the price and ATC at the quantity where MR = MC.
why: The profit draws rivals in. Each new rival takes some of this firm's buyers, so its demand shifts left until the profit is gone.

scenarios.title: Long-run equilibrium
scenarios.cause: Rivals have entered until no firm earns an economic profit.

point.label: M
point.ask: the firm's quantity and price in the long run.
point.why: where MR = MC, priced on demand, which now just touches ATC there: P = ATC.

check.label: Compared with the bottom of its ATC, where does the firm produce in the long run?
options: At a smaller quantity: it has excess capacity, and its price is above MC
At the bottom of ATC, like a perfectly competitive firm
At a larger quantity, past the bottom of ATC
Where demand meets MC
why: Yes. Its demand slopes down, so it touches ATC on the falling part of ATC: output is below the bottom of ATC and P = ATC > MC.
Only a firm with a horizontal demand curve ends at the bottom of ATC. This one's demand slopes down.
The tangency is on the falling part of ATC, to the left of its bottom.
That would be allocative efficiency; the firm makes less, where MR = MC.

scenarios.title: Deadweight loss
scenarios.cause: The firm charges its profit-maximizing price.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The firm stops where MR = MC, short of where demand meets MC: the triangle between demand and MC over those units.

scenarios.title: The product sells for more
scenarios.cause: Demand for the {firm}'s product rises, so its price rises.
scenarios.because: a higher product price raising MRP
scenarios.askShift: Shift every curve this change moves: in the market and at the firm.

slips.SL: The product price changes what each worker's output is worth to employers (MRP = MP x P), not how many people want the job: it shifts labor demand, and each firm's MRP with it.

line.why: The firm takes the new market wage: its labor supply is the horizontal line S = MFC = W at that wage.

point.label: H
point.ask: how many workers the firm hires now.
point.why: where its MRP crosses the wage line: MRP = MRC.

why: Every link: product demand rises, the product price rises, so MRP = MP x P rises, so the demand for labor shifts right.

scenarios.title: More productive workers
scenarios.cause: New tools let each {job} make more in an hour.
scenarios.askShift: Shift every curve this change moves: in the market and at the firm.

line.why: The firm takes the new, higher market wage.

point.label: H
point.ask: how many workers the firm hires now.
point.why: where its new MRP crosses the new wage line.

scenarios.title: More workers
scenarios.cause: Many trained {job}s move to the region.

slips.DL: More workers changes labor supply, not what each worker is worth to employers: supply shifts right.
slips.MRP: The firm's MRP depends on productivity and the product price, which did not change; the market's labor supply shifts.

line.why: The firm takes the new, lower market wage.

point.label: H
point.ask: how many workers the firm hires now.
point.why: where its MRP crosses the lower wage line: more workers than before.

scenarios.title: How many to hire
scenarios.cause: The {firm} takes the market wage as given.

point.label: H
point.ask: how many workers the firm hires.
point.why: where MRP meets the wage line: hire while the next worker adds at least as much revenue as she costs.

check.label: For a firm selling in a competitive product market, MRP equals:
options: The marginal product of labor times the product price
The wage times the number of workers
Marginal revenue times the product price
The total product divided by the number of workers
why: Yes. MRP = MP x MR, and for a price taker MR is the price.
That is the wage bill, what the firm pays in all.
MRP multiplies MR by the marginal product, not by the price.
That is the average product of labor.

scenarios.title: The monopsony's choice
scenarios.cause: The only employer chooses how many {job}s to hire and what to pay.

point.label: H
point.ask: the number hired and the wage paid.
point.why: at the number where MRP = MFC, with the wage read down on the labor supply curve at that number.

check.label: Why is MFC above the labor supply curve?
options: To hire one more worker the firm must raise the wage for everyone it employs
Because each new worker is less productive
Because the firm pays more than the market wage to be fair
Because labor supply slopes down
why: Yes. The extra worker costs her own wage plus the raise for all the others, so the marginal cost of a worker is above the wage.
Falling marginal product bends MRP down; it does not raise MFC.
The monopsonist pays the lowest wage the supply curve allows.
Labor supply slopes up: more workers come only at a higher wage.

scenarios.title: The wage bill
scenarios.cause: The monopsonist hires where MRP = MFC.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The wage bill is the wage times the workers hired: the rectangle under the monopsony wage, out to the number hired.

scenarios.title: Deadweight loss of monopsony
scenarios.cause: The monopsonist hires fewer workers than a competitive market would.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The workers not hired would have added more (MRP) than the least they would accept (labor supply): the triangle between MRP and labor supply over those workers.

scenarios.title: The product sells for more
scenarios.cause: The price of what the employer sells rises.
scenarios.because: a higher product price raising MRP

slips.SL: The product price changes what each worker is worth to the firm, MRP, not how many people want to work there.

point.label: H
point.ask: the new number hired and wage.
point.why: where the new MRP meets MFC, with the wage read down on labor supply.

scenarios.title: If the market were competitive
scenarios.cause: Suppose many employers competed for these workers instead.

point.label: C
point.ask: the wage and employment a competitive market would reach.
point.why: where MRP (labor demand) meets labor supply: more workers at a higher wage than under monopsony.

scenarios.title: Pollution
scenarios.setting: A paper mill dumps waste into a river, harming people downstream.
scenarios.cause: Each unit of paper made imposes a cost on others that the mill does not pay.

point.label: E
point.ask: the efficient quantity and price.
point.why: where MSB = MSC. The market makes more, where demand meets private supply.

scenarios.shadeWhy: The units between the efficient and the market quantity cost society more (MSC) than they are worth (MSB): the triangle between MSC and demand over those units.

scenarios.title: What the market makes
scenarios.setting: A factory's smoke harms its neighbors.
scenarios.cause: The factory sells its output in a market that ignores the harm.

point.label: M
point.ask: the quantity and price the market reaches.
point.why: where demand (MPB) meets supply (MPC): the market ignores the external cost, so it makes more than the efficient quantity.

scenarios.title: Vaccination
scenarios.setting: Each flu shot also protects the people around the person who gets it.
scenarios.cause: Buyers count only their own benefit.

point.label: E
point.ask: the efficient quantity and price.
point.why: where MSB = MSC. The market makes less, where private demand meets supply.

scenarios.shadeWhy: The units between the market and the efficient quantity are worth more to society (MSB) than they cost (MSC), but are not made: the triangle between MSB and supply over those units.

scenarios.title: Beekeeping
scenarios.setting: A beekeeper's bees pollinate the orchards nearby.
scenarios.cause: The beekeeper is not paid for the pollination.

point.label: E
point.ask: the efficient quantity and price.
point.why: where demand meets MSC, below private supply: the efficient quantity is larger than the market's.

scenarios.title: A corrective tax
scenarios.setting: A chemical plant's runoff harms a lake.
scenarios.cause: The government taxes each unit by the external cost it imposes.
scenarios.because: a per-unit tax equal to the external cost
scenarios.askShift: Show the tax: shift the curve it moves, the way it moves it.

slips.D: The tax is on producers, so it raises their cost of each unit: supply shifts left, onto MSC.

why: A tax equal to the external cost makes sellers pay the full social cost, so supply moves onto MSC and the market reaches the efficient quantity.

scenarios.title: A corrective subsidy
scenarios.setting: Each flu shot also protects other people.
scenarios.cause: The government pays buyers a subsidy per shot equal to the external benefit.
scenarios.because: a per-unit subsidy to buyers equal to the external benefit
scenarios.askShift: Show the subsidy: shift the curve it moves, the way it moves it.

slips.S: This subsidy goes to buyers, so it raises what each shot is worth to them: demand shifts right, onto MSB.

why: A subsidy to buyers equal to the external benefit makes demand count the whole social benefit, so the market reaches the efficient quantity.

scenarios.title: Progressive taxes and transfers
scenarios.cause: The country raises taxes on high incomes and pays cash transfers to low-income households.
why: Moving income from the top to the bottom brings the Lorenz curve closer to the line of equality, and the Gini coefficient falls.

scenarios.title: Wages pull apart
scenarios.cause: Pay for the highest-paid jobs rises much faster than pay for everyone else.
why: The top earns a larger share, so the curve bows farther from the line of equality and the Gini coefficient rises.

scenarios.title: The Gini area
scenarios.cause: Measure how unequal incomes are.
scenarios.ask: Shade the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve.
scenarios.shadeWhy: The Gini coefficient is this area divided by the whole triangle under the line of equality: 0 means perfect equality, close to 1 means one household has nearly all the income.
